Also, for Kabbalistic reasons, you should look at your palm – and specifically not look at your thumb. The best way to do this is as we described above – curling your fingers over your palm, with your thumb tucked in, and viewing both together. Many then open their hand up, signifying that light will penetrate the darkness. They also turn their hand around while opening it and look at their nails once more from behind. (It’s also brought down not to look at the inner side of your fingers at this time, only the side with the nails.) This is all done with the right hand (although some repeat the same motion with their left).
This also applies to the person making Havdalah. Before smelling the spices (besamim), he should move the cup of wine from his right hand to his left, hold the spices in his right, make the blessing on them, and smell them. He should then keep the cup in his left hand while he blesses the fire and looks at his nails. This way, he too will look at the nails on his right hand. Afterwards, he returns the cup to his right hand and concludes Havdalah.
There is also a question if to look at your nails before the blessing on the fire is recited or right after. The more common custom is to look at your nails only after the blessing is said, although even better is to look at your nails both times. (This is what I do, but I only do the motion of opening my hand and looking at the back of my hand after the blessing, not before.)
Lastly, there doesn't seem to be any source for the notion of holding the candle as high as you want your future spouse to be. I know someone who used to meticulously hold the family’s Havdalah candle at about 5’11” from the ground. I commented to her that considering that she was already well into her twenties, her future husband has most likely already reached his full height, and it’s hard to believe that holding the Havdalah candle at a specific height will make the slightest difference! (Thankfully, she is long happily married – though to a man somewhat shorter than her target height.)
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch O.C. 298:3; Be’er Heitev 4; Mishna Berurah 9-11; The Radiance of Shabbos, pp. 138-139.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: The Secret of Happiness Hidden in the Sukkah
questions.question: The Secret of Happiness Hidden in the Sukkah

answers.text:
The Israelites left Egypt with no food, no water and no plan. Then they stumbled on a campsite that had been waiting for them.
The Torah calls Sukkot "the time of our joy." This is the festival meant to teach us how to be happy in the world.
Strangely, though, we don't do anything obviously happy. We leave our homes and move into a sukkah, a hut with a roof so flimsy it isn't even waterproof. What does that have to do with happiness?
The Book of Leviticus (23:43) explains the reason for the holiday: "So that your future generations will know that I placed the Children of Israel in sukkot (huts) when I took them out of the land of Egypt."
There's just one problem. The Torah never describes the Israelites living in sukkot when God took them out of Egypt. Throughout the 40 years in the desert, whenever the Torah mentions where they lived, it's always an ohel, a tent. Never a sukkah.
So how do we make sense of this? I want to share an idea I find very exciting, but first, one more critical question.
The Talmud says that when God speaks of placing us in sukkot, it could mean either physical huts, which the Torah never mentions, or the Clouds of Glory, which it does. A special cloud surrounded the people and protected them on their journey through the desert. But how does a hut connect to a cloud?
I said the Torah never mentions the Israelites dwelling in sukkot. But if we read carefully, there is one moment where it does. The Torah tells us they traveled to a place called Sukkot: "The Children of Israel journeyed from Ramses to Sukkot" (Exodus 12:37).
Why would a place be called Sukkot? Interestingly, the Torah mentions another place with the same name, in a completely different region. When Jacob returns to the Land of Israel, he too comes to a place called Sukkot.
Bible critics argued that the Egyptian Sukkot must be a mistake. We can locate it on the map. Today it's known as Tjeku, and excavations show there was no settlement there when the Israelites left Egypt. It wasn't a city.
James Hoffmeier, one of the world's leading experts in Egyptian archaeology, says the critics have it backwards. Of course the Israelites wouldn't escape Egyptian slavery and head straight into an Egyptian city. If Tjeku had been built up, they would have avoided it. They went there precisely because it wasn't.
What Tjeku was, at the time of the Exodus, was an old campsite. In earlier times, Semitic peoples sometimes migrated from Canaan down to Egypt. Travelers needed places with food, water, and people to trade with. Tjeku had been a massive Semitic transit camp.
Now picture the scene. The Israelites are leaving Egypt with no provisions and no idea what lies ahead. Pharaoh has told them to go. Moses has told them to follow him. It's a tremendous leap of faith. They head out into the desert and the questions start: What will we eat? What will we drink? Where will we even sleep tonight?
Suddenly they arrive at an old campsite, full of huts that had been standing there for decades, maybe centuries, along with materials to build more. "In sukkot I made the Israelites dwell when I took them out of Egypt," God says, on that very night.
Imagine being one of those Israelites and seeing a place that had been waiting for you. It was God's way of saying, "I've got you covered. You'll be looked after. You're not taking this journey alone. I'm with you every step of the way." And it was there that the Clouds of Glory descended and carried them through the rest of the journey.
So when we sit in the sukkah, we remember that first night out of Egypt, when God had prepared a place for us and showed us He would carry us forward. And we remember the Clouds of Glory, which came down that day at Sukkot and led us the rest of the way.
This reveals something remarkable. Every place in the Torah called Sukkot is a transit camp, a place you stop on the way somewhere else.
And that's the secret of life. The more we try to stand still, the less life works for us. The more we accept that life is a journey, the more incredible it becomes.
Being on a journey means you're growing. It means you're not trying to stay put. It means you're trying to become a better person. We just had Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. We had deep moments, powerful dreams, real desire to change. But no one changes in a day. So take those dreams and ask yourself, "Who am I going to be a year from now?" Then, just like the Israelites heading into the desert, begin the journey one step at a time.
What was my dream on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur? Who did I think I could become? Write it down. Set goals. Then start walking. One small step in that direction, then another, then another.
That's where life's true joy lies: in growing, in heading somewhere, in living with meaning and purpose, in actually becoming something. When all we try to do is make ourselves comfortable, there's no deep fulfillment in it. But when we're taking steps, growing, moving toward a destination, that's where simcha, true joy, comes from.
And when we know God is walking with us every step of the way, we know we're on the right path, the path to greatness. We don't need to be perfect. We don't need to have arrived. The joy is in the journey itself.
As we sit in our sukkahs this year, may we travel back in time and feel the magic of that first night. Feel the Israelites' fear, and their elation, knowing they were marching one step at a time, not only out of Egypt toward the Land of Israel, and not only away from their troubles, but toward building all of history. May God accompany each of us on our own journeys, and may this be a true time of simcha, of joy.

questions.title: The Toy Torah a Soldier Found in Gaza
questions.question: The Toy Torah a Soldier Found in Gaza

answers.text:
Terrorists fleeing Khan Yunis left behind guns, ammunition, and a child's stuffed holiday toy. One Israeli soldier carried it from Gaza to Lebanon to keep a promise.
It’s an incongruous site: An Israeli soldier stands amid the rubble of a building in Lebanon, holding a child's plush Torah scroll.
It is the kind of toy children receive for Simchat Torah, so they can join the joyous dancing with a Torah of their own. This toy Torah scroll traveled through the darkest chapter in recent Jewish history.
After the Hamas invasion and massacre on October 7, 2023, Avi Kramer and his unit were sent into Gaza. He served in the IDF Paratroopers Brigade's 202nd Battalion, known as the Viper Battalion.
Avi's role was search and rescue. If a soldier was wounded, he would enter the firefight and extract him to safety.
For the first months of the war, Avi was stationed inside Gaza, returning to Israel for only a few days each month. Toward the end of 2023, his unit was operating in Khan Yunis, a major Hamas stronghold in the southern Gaza Strip and the hometown of Yahya Sinwar, the architect of the October 7 attack.
Beneath the city, Hamas had built an extensive network of tunnels, weapons facilities and command centers. Israeli hostages were also held there. Avi's unit was in the midst of rooting out terrorists when his fellow soldiers searched a seemingly ordinary apartment.
There were signs that terrorists had been there only a day earlier. Apparently fleeing as the IDF closed in, they left behind guns, ammunition and combat gear.
Then Avi heard a soldier's excited voice crackle over the radio: "I found a child's toy," the soldier called out. "A stuffed Torah scroll.”
Simchat Torah is one of the most joyous days of the Jewish year. Adults dance in synagogue with Torah scrolls, while children wave flags, ride on their parents' shoulders and carry toy Torahs of their own.
On Simchat Torah 2023, that dancing was shattered by sirens, gunfire, murder, and kidnappings.
That plush toy, embroidered with the words "Rejoice and celebrate on Simchat Torah” (Sisu v'simchu b'Simchat Torah), was a remnant of a celebration interrupted, a people attacked – and a childhood violated.
Avi asked the soldiers who had found it if he could keep it. Strictly speaking, it was not a holy object. Yet it was, for him, a silent witness to October 7 and a symbol of everything the terrorists had tried to steal.
“The soldiers agreed to give me the toy as their way of showing appreciation," Avi says.
That day in Khan Yunis, that little Torah was returned to Jewish hands.
No one knows how this child's toy reached Khan Yunis. Had it belonged to a child kidnapped into Gaza? Had a terrorist looted it from Sderot, Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz, or another community overrun that morning?
Avi on the vehicle used to evacuate wounded IDF soldiers during combat.
Avi can only speculate about why a terrorist might have taken it. "Perhaps it was a memento," he says, "their way of saying, 'We've defeated the Jewish people who live by the Torah.'"
Yet Avi knew that October 7 was not the end of the story. The Jewish people would reach another Simchat Torah. They would hold the Torah again and, despite the grief, they would dance.
Avi placed the toy in his pack and, a few months later, carried it out of Gaza. Then he made himself a promise: At the next Simchat Torah, I will dance with this Torah.
A few days before Sukkot 2024, Avi was called back to reserve duty, this time to enter Lebanon and fight Hezbollah. He had little time to pack, but he made sure to bring the toy Torah.
At the army base, busy preparing for the mission, Avi had no time to build a proper sukkah, so he assembled a few beams and made a makeshift one.
His unit remained in Lebanon throughout the seven-day Sukkot holiday. Simchat Torah, which followed, was especially painful: it marked the first Hebrew-calendar anniversary of the Hamas massacre. Hostages remained in captivity, families were mourning, communities were displaced, and soldiers continued to fall.
Still, Avi and his fellow soldiers wanted to observe Simchat Torah with dancing. Yet at their makeshift army base, they needed to be very quiet and keep the lights out.
They had no genuine Torah scroll. So they danced in near-silence with the stuffed one. Surrounded by the wreckage of war, Avi fulfilled his promise.
A year later, on Hoshana Rabba 2025, the final 20 living hostages were released from Gaza. The next day, Simchat Torah, Avi celebrated with friends near Meron in northern Israel, a place with special meaning for him: He had been there on the day of the Hamas attack exactly two years earlier.
This time, Avi danced with a real Torah scroll – and with the stuffed one, grieving yet still dancing, carrying the Torah forward. Terrorists could not take ownership of the Jewish story.
That little Torah, carried into Gaza as a trophy of cruelty, was redeemed as a symbol of Jewish determination, resilience, and faith.
"My hope and prayer," Avi says, "is that one day, when I'm married and have a family of my own, my child will dance with that same toy scroll."

questions.title: An Oct 7 Hero's Widow Marries Her Husband’s Former Commander
questions.question: An Oct 7 Hero's Widow Marries Her Husband’s Former Commander

answers.text:
Out of the pain of October 7, a young widow found the courage to love again. Her wedding showed what makes the Jewish people unbreakable.
Beneath a wedding canopy near Ma’ale Adumim on June 23, 2026, Miriam stood beside Ofek, preparing to begin a new chapter in her life.
They were surrounded by family, friends, music, and celebration, but also by tears. Present in every heart was the memory of Captain Ori Mordechai Shani, Miriam’s first husband, the father of her little boy, Roi, and a former soldier under Ofek Datan’s command.
Ori was not physically there, yet everyone could feel his presence.
Miriam and Or Shani were a beautiful young couple, deeply in love and filled with dreams for their future. Together, they built a home grounded in faith, devotion, and love. When their son, Roi, was born, they imagined all the ordinary and precious moments their family would share.
Roi was only four months old when their world was shattered.
just 22 years old, Ori served as a platoon commander in the Golani Brigade’s 51st Battalion. On the morning of October 7, Ori and five of his soldiers left the Kissufim IDF outpost for a routine patrol. When Hamas terrorists invaded Israel, they found themselves facing a heavily armed force. Despite limited ammunition and equipment, Ori remained calm and courageous, leading his men through hours of intense fighting and helping prevent the terrorists from advancing toward Kibbutz Kissufim.
Under relentless fire, Ori guided his soldiers safely back to the base to replenish their ammunition. There, however, Ori and one of his soldiers, Sergeant Re’em Batito, were tragically killed in a mortar attack.
In recognition of his extraordinary courage, leadership, and sacrifice, Ori was posthumously promoted to the rank of captain.
In a single moment, Miriam lost the man she loved, the father of her infant son, and the partner with whom she had planned her future. She now had to look into her baby’s eyes, knowing that he would grow up without his father’s embrace, while somehow finding the strength to face each new day.
Some forms of grief are too deep for words. They do not simply disappear with time, they become part of the person who carries them.
Miriam continued to care for Roi and learned to take one-step and then another. She carried Ori with her, not only in photographs and memories, but as a living presence within her heart. She has described the love he left inside her as a love that will never end and will always remain part of who she is.
Miriam found love with Ofek Dotan, who had been Ori’s commander during his training in the Egoz Unit. Ofek understood the depth of her loss and knew that loving Miriam meant making room for Ori’s memory, never competing with it or trying to replace it.
With the loving support of Ori’s family, Miriam chose to open her heart again.
During their wedding ceremony, Ofek addressed Ori. He recalled how Ori had once told him about Miriam, how deeply he loved her and how excited he was to build a home with her.
Ofek thanked Ori for building the “first floor” of that home. He described the life he and Miriam were now creating as a “second floor”, built upon the strong foundations Ori had laid.
It was an extraordinary expression of tenderness and humility - the new home did not erase the first, it rose from it.
That moment captured something profound about the Jewish people.
For centuries, our small nation has endured persecution, exile, terror, and unimaginable loss. Again and again, we have been broken, yet we have refused to remain among the ruins. We have answered death with life, destruction with rebuilding, and hatred with an even greater commitment to love.
Choosing life does not mean forgetting those we have lost. It means carrying them forward with us. Miriam’s love for Ofek does not diminish the love she will always carry for Ori. Her wedding was not the end of her grief; it was her courageous decision not to allow grief to be the end of her story.
It is planting a tree where fire once burned, building a home where another was shattered, and standing beneath a chuppah with tears in our eyes and hope in our hearts.
We do not rise because we were never broken. We rise because, even after being broken, we gather the pieces and begin to build again.
It is an act of faith, an act of defiance, and one of the greatest acts of courage.

questions.title: My Birthday Is October 7th
questions.question: My Birthday Is October 7th

answers.text:
My birthday is October 7th, and I refuse to stop celebrating it. In fact, I believe we were all reborn that day.
I have a birthday twin in L.A. We were both born on the same day, in the same year.
After that infamous day in 2023, my friend told me she would never celebrate her birthday on October 7th again.
When I tell people I was born on October 7th, their reaction is usually one of three things: silence, a gasp, or a sad, “Ohhh…”
And then I tell them: There are no accidents or coincidences.
October 7th was a wake-up call of seismic proportions for all of us.
October 7th was a wake-up call of seismic proportions for all of us.
I am not hiding from my birthday. I am not shunning it. I am embracing it as a powerful message from Above—because I believe all of life is filled with messages, if we are willing to see them.
October 7th was a wake-up call of seismic proportions for all of us.
It wasn't the first time a crisis forced open a door we'd rather have kept shut.
During the lockdowns of Covid, a spotlight was suddenly turned on inside our homes.
Some of what we saw was beautiful: families reconnecting, playing board games, baking bread, appreciating one another, protecting and cherishing the elderly.
One woman called me and said, “I always knew my husband drank a little too much. But now that we’re locked down together, I realize my husband is an alcoholic. Is my marriage over?”
“No,” I reassured her. “Your marriage isn’t over. Let’s be grateful that you know. Now let’s get you some help.”
Another woman reached out to me: “Lori, I thought I had a great relationship with my son. But now that he’s home with us through Covid… well, I think my son hates me. What do I do?”
I told her the first thing she needed to do was thank God that she knew.
Because knowing the truth—even when it hurts—is the beginning of being able to change it.
October 7th jolted us, in the most horrific way imaginable, into a reality many of us had been unwilling—or unable—to fully see.
The antisemitism was there all along. It was painful to discover that much of it had simply been waiting for an opportunity to reveal itself.
The antisemitism was there all along. It was painful to discover that much of it had simply been waiting for an opportunity to reveal itself.
The antisemitism was there all along. It was painful to discover that much of it had simply been waiting for an opportunity to reveal itself.
But would we rather be blind and not know? Would we rather look away?
There are moments in a person’s life when you suddenly find out who your real friends are.
It can happen after a divorce, a financial loss, a prolonged illness, or another crisis.
A woman I know got divorced and discovered that most of her “friends” sided with her wealthy husband.
I told her something that may sound harsh, but I believe is true:
More painful than discovering that these people weren’t her true friends would have been going through life believing that they were.
Yes, my birthday is October 7th. And after the initial reaction I described above, I tell everyone:
If we are not different people and a different nation after that day—if our existing organizations don’t wipe their boards clean, rethink what they are doing, and reimagine what they can become—then what was it all for?
We cannot, and should not, simply “go back to the way it was.”
The question is not only: What happened to us on October 7th?
The question is: What are we going to do with what happened to us?
I cannot answer these questions for you I can only answer them for me and make a few suggestions:
I’ve already moved to Israel and now I am louder than ever that this is the place to be. If you are not living here now, take a step towards it, have that conversation with friends and family. You may be surprised that they may be considering it too. In the meantime, visit! It’s the home of your soul and the ultimate family reunion.
For most of us, our Bar are Bat Mitzvahs were our graduations out of Jewish learning, instead of our graduations in. Decide now to take a second look at your heritage that changed the world for all time. We are “the people of the book”—let’s read it! The week of October 7th this year falls on the week we all begin reading the parsha from page one again…together. Be part of the greatest “book club” ever.
Judaism is not a spectator sport. Like Nike, we must DO IT! It’s not all or nothing, so pick a mitzvah you have been thinking about doing and make it your own. Lighting shabbat candles, putting on tefillin, saying the Shema every day, giving tzedakah… Raise the bar 10% every year and soon you’ll be soaring high.
A wake-up call is only useful if we wake up…and really change.

questions.title: The World Says You're a Jew. Now What?
questions.question: The World Says You're a Jew. Now What?

answers.text:
At NYU, my nephew took a stand and lost friends overnight. He knew why he was targeted but no one ever explained to him why being Jewish was worth it.
On the morning of October 7, 2023, my nephew, a student at NYU, woke up and reached for his phone. His feed was already flooded with posts attacking Israel. He didn't yet know what had happened there.
Only after scrolling through post after post did he piece together what had happened hours earlier. Hamas terrorists had crossed into Israel, murdered some 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and dragged 251 hostages into Gaza.
Like many Jewish college students, he had a Jewish life, but it wasn’t the center of his identity. He attended Jewish events and the occasional Shabbaton, and moved easily between his Jewish and non-Jewish worlds. Being Jewish was part of who he was. He just never assumed it was how other people saw him.
That changed quickly, as other people began drawing the line for him. Within days, posters went up around campus with the faces of the hostages: grandparents, mothers, teenagers, and dozens of children, some of them babies, taken from their homes and held in tunnels under Gaza by Hamas.
The posters appealed to a basic human instinct: whatever anyone thought about the Middle East, surely no one could look at the photograph of a kidnapped four-year-old and feel nothing.
His response triggered a deluge of hate messages, many of them from people he knew and had thought were his friends.
His response triggered a deluge of hate messages, many of them from people he knew and had thought were his friends.
Yet the posters were torn down, again and again. When the university suspended a student for ripping them off the walls, my nephew posted that the school had made the right call.
His response triggered a deluge of hate messages, many of them from people he knew and had thought were his friends. They defended the student who had torn the posters down and called my nephew Islamophobic, as though what bothered him was the student’s religion rather than the sight of kidnapped Jews being stripped off the walls. Many of those friendships ended right there, and the campus environment became so toxic for him that he went abroad the next semester.
When I talked with him afterward, what struck me most was how well he held up. He didn’t fold, and he didn’t quietly wonder whether the crowd had a point. He was shocked that so many educated people had lost the ability to tell right from wrong on something so plain.
He was singled out because he was a Jew. But he had no sense of what being a Jew is for, and why it might be worth everything it was suddenly costing him.
He was singled out because he was a Jew. But he had no sense of what being a Jew is for, and why it might be worth everything it was suddenly costing him.
He knew he had been singled out because he was a Jew. But no one had given him a sense of what being a Jew is for, and why it might be worth everything it was suddenly costing him.
The world has spent the last three years telling Jews, loudly and clearly, that they are Jews. But what is less clear is who gets to decide what it means, the people shouting at them or the Jews themselves? How we answer that question will shape the Jewish future more than any campus policy or election.
For decades after the Holocaust, many Jews, especially in the West, believed that antisemitism had been pushed to the margins. It was ugly and it still existed, but it belonged to cranks and to history. Respectable people didn’t go there.
Then came October 7. Before Israel had buried its dead, and before a single soldier had entered Gaza, crowds were in the streets of major cities, and they had not come to mourn. The old hatred hadn’t disappeared after all; it simply found new expression - in the language of human rights, anti-colonialism and social justice, and with it a new respectability on campuses, in newsrooms and across professional life.
But what it said to Jews was very old. It didn’t matter whether you had ever been to Israel, voted there, or held any opinion about its government. No one asks Chinese-American students to denounce Beijing’s treatment of the Uyghurs before they are welcome at the lunch table, yet Jewish students were expected to disavow the Jewish state as the price of belonging. It has often been said that Israel has become the Jew among the nations; the reverse is just as true, and every Jew is now treated as Israel’s ambassador, whether he signed up for the job or not.
People who had given little thought to what it means to be Jewish were suddenly being asked to account for it by classmates, colleagues and strangers.
People who had given little thought to what it means to be Jewish were suddenly being asked to account for it by classmates, colleagues and strangers.
One of the stranger results of these three years is that people who had given little thought to what it means to be Jewish were suddenly being asked to account for it by classmates, colleagues and strangers, and every one of them has had to decide what to do about it.
In 1946, in the book published in English as Anti-Semite and Jew, Jean-Paul Sartre wrote that “the Jew is one whom other men consider a Jew.” He meant it as part of an attack on antisemitism, and his argument was that the antisemite, in effect, creates the Jew. For a secular Jew, that can feel uncomfortably accurate: you are Jewish because the world won’t let you forget it.
It is also a trap, and Sartre himself came to see it. His account, for all its good intentions, left the Jews nothing of their own, no history, faith or purpose beyond being hated. Late in life, in conversations with his secretary Benny Lévy, who was returning to Judaism, Sartre acknowledged that the Jews have a real history and hope of their own, one no antisemite wrote for them.
If your identity is whatever your enemies say it is, you have handed them the pen.
If your identity is whatever your enemies say it is, you have handed them the pen.
If your identity is whatever your enemies say it is, you have handed them the pen. To a large degree that is what has happened for the past two generations. Much of Diaspora Jewish identity has been built on the Holocaust and on the fight against antisemitism. Remembering is a sacred duty, but when the story you tell your children is mainly about the people who hated you, you have in effect let them write it. A Jewishness built on being hated has little positive to teach your children, and little to offer them except a reason to walk away.
Jewish tradition makes the opposite claim. When the prophet Bilaam was hired to curse Israel, he looked at the people and said instead: Am levadad yishkon, "a nation that dwells alone" (Numbers 23:9). What was meant as a curse came out as a blessing, describing not a people cut off from the world but one whose sense of itself doesn't depend on the world's approval.
An earlier generation went through something similar. The Jews of Persia in the Purim story were comfortable, hobnobbing with the non-Jews in the capital Shushan as they attended the king’s feast. Then Haman described them to the king as “a certain people, scattered and dispersed among the nations, whose laws are different” (Esther 3:8), and a decree for genocide went out to kill “all the Jews, young and old” (3:13). Haman made no distinction between the observant and the assimilated; to him, a Jew was a Jew.
The Talmud (Shabbat 88a) makes a remarkable claim about what happened next. At Sinai, the Jewish people had accepted the Torah under a kind of compulsion, but now in the days of Purim and Achashverosh they accepted it again, freely. This is the meaning of the phrase in the Megillah, kiymu v’kiblu (Esther 9:27), “they upheld and accepted,” which the Talmud reads to mean that they now upheld with love what they had long before accepted more from a sense of fear.
The generation that finally embraced the Torah with a full heart was the very one that had just been told by the most powerful empire on earth that they were Jews and would die for it.
The generation that finally embraced the Torah with a full heart was the very one that had just been told by the most powerful empire on earth that they were Jews and would die for it.
Consider this: the generation that finally embraced the Torah with a full heart was the very one that had just been told by the most powerful empire on earth that they were Jews and would die for it. They could have treated their Jewishness as a liability to be minimized; instead, they answered by defining themselves.
Some Jews have distanced themselves. This is the familiar “As a Jew” declaration, assuring the world that they are not that kind of Jew. Privately, it may be nothing more dramatic than a necklace tucked beneath a shirt or silence in the group chat.
I don't judge anyone who is afraid, but distance buys less than it promises because the people demanding it rarely stop at the first concession.
Others, like my nephew, have stood their ground. That takes real courage, but resistance alone is still reactive. It may carry you through a hostile semester; it is harder to build a Jewish life on, much less pass one to your children.
And some Jews have gone deeper. They stopped asking, “Why do they hate us?” and began asking, ”What is it about being Jewish that has been worth carrying for all these centuries?” They opened a page of Torah or a book of Jewish history, came to a Shabbat table, and went to Israel to stand with family Jews who never thought of themselves as religious are lighting Shabbat candles, baking challah, signing up for classes and turning up at shul for the first time in years. This is the response of Shushan, taking an identity the world forced on us and choosing it for ourselves.
This response lasts because it is built on who you are rather than on who hates you. That identity is yours to create, and every Jew who chooses to learn, to celebrate, to show up, becomes part of a story that has outlasted every enemy who tried to end it.

questions.title: From Abraham to October 7th: A New Book on Israel's Modern Heroes
questions.question: From Abraham to October 7th: A New Book on Israel's Modern Heroes

answers.text:
A soldier ran 8 miles in wet clothes to join the fight. A mother drew terrorists away from her child. David Kramer sees ancient Jewish heroes living again.
David Kramer’s new book, History’s Greatest Comeback: How the Ancient Stories of the Bible Are Unfolding in Israel Today, draws parallels between the heroes of the recent war and Biblical heroes, tracing the arc of Jewish history and a vision for a brighter future.
David tells the story of Avichail Reuven, a soldier whose family had come to Israel from Ethiopia. On October 7th, Avichail was home for Shabbat. David says, “He put his clothes in the wash, and he is with his family, and they get news of what’s happening. Avichail didn’t have a car. He just packed up and said, I’m going. He took his clothes out – they were still wet – and he literally ran 8 miles to the south of Israel. He never knew where he was going; he just ran. He was so determined to get there and to help, and I think just that act alone is incredible.”
Eventually, Avichail reached the Zikim army base and was instrumental in retaking the base from terrorists. He went on to serve for the next three years, fighting in Gaza. “Today, he’s been promoted to quite a high-ranking officer,” says David.
To David, Avichail’s story parallels that of Patriarch Abraham, who went through many trials and “never knew what the end would be. They all had an element of life and death, and he never knew that he was going to make it at the end of the trial. That faith, knowing that no matter what, I'm going to do it because that's what God wants from me, I think that's exactly what motivated Avichail. He never knew whether he was going to make it at the end of the day, but he went through everything just to help his brothers and sisters, knowing that God was going to be with him.”
Another example of a modern-day heroine is Yarden Roman-Gat, whom David compares to the Biblical Queen Esther, who “didn’t seek heroism, it found her. She could have remained silent,” but she chose to act.
Similarly, when on October 7th, Yarden, her husband Alon, and their three-year-old daughter were abducted from their home, Yarden chose to act. As the terrorists holding them neared the Gaza border, Yarden “handed her daughter to Alon and ran in a different direction, diverting the terrorists so her husband and child could escape,” wrote David.
Though Yarden was captured and spent two months in captivity in Gaza, her husband managed to escape to safety with their daughter.
David was inspired to write his book at the funeral of Corporal Daniel Perez, a South African-born tank commander killed in battle on October 7th.
Originally from Johannesburg, South Africa, David has known the Perez family for decades. Daniel’s father, Rabbi Doron Perez, currently president of the World Zionist Organization, had been David’s youth counselor back in South Africa, and David has maintained a close relationship with him ever since.
In his book, David compares Daniel to the Maccabees, who “taught us that true bravery has never been measured by weapons or might but by conviction alone.” Like the Maccabees, fueled by conviction and commitment to protect his people, Daniel fought against a much stronger enemy.
David tells Daniel’s story: “On October 7, Daniel commanded his tank at the Nahal Oz outpost, one of the first and hardest-hit positions in the Hamas onslaught. For two hours and sixteen minutes, Daniel and his crew fought against overwhelming odds.” They saved dozens of lives. “Daniel was a real hero,” says David.
After Daniel was killed, his body was abducted by Hamas terrorists and taken to Gaza. At first, it was not known whether Daniel was still alive. In March 2024, his blood-soaked uniform was discovered, and the rabbinate declared Daniel’s death, based on the amount of blood. David says, “I remember being at his first funeral, where there were thousands of people that came from all over.”
When Daniel’s body was released two years later in the last hostage exchange, an announcement came out that there would be a second funeral. David recalls, “Because I'm close to the family, I said, I better go. I don't know how many people will come to the second funeral. And when I got there, I just couldn't believe it. Again, there were thousands of people who came from all over the country. I remember standing among Daniel’s friends, these boys who had become warriors and led the war throughout these years. In front of me was the former chief of staff, Herzi Halevi, talking to the father of Hirsch Goldberg Polin, another hostage who was murdered in captivity. I could only imagine what they were saying to each other. And then in front of me was the president of Israel, and the generals, and other dignitaries.”
The most poignant moment of the second funeral was when “Matan Angrest walked in,” recalls David. Matan was one of Daniel's tank crew members, captured alive and taken to Gaza on October 7th and released only three days earlier. “There was a moment at this funeral that was just transcendent,” says David. “There was something that I'd never experienced before.”
Matan Angrest giving a eulogy at Daniel Perez’s second funeral
Looking around the military cemetery at the graves of other fallen soldiers, David “was overcome with this incredible sense of pride: pride in what this little tiny nation has achieved, pride in the fact that this country's so resilient and so strong, and that we got through. And more than that, I felt, we've got one of the most incredible stories to tell.” David’s new book is full of such inspiring stories.
David Kramer leading a group of students at Daniel Perez's grave
For the front cover of his book, David selected a kalanit, the red flower that grows throughout the south of Israel. “You could only imagine what this little flower witnessed on October 7th, when thousands of terrorists came over the border,” says David. “This little flower was trampled on, but it has grown again. It's back in the thousands in the south of Israel, just like the Jewish people. Throughout the years, that's been our story. People have tried to destroy us, to trample us, to cancel us. And yet, year after year, the Jewish people keep coming back.”
David applies the same principle to the Jewish communities outside of Israel. After a terrorist attack, whether in America, Britain, or Australia, “the Jews are back in synagogue the next week, they're lighting Shabbat candles, they're lighting Chanukah candles,” says David. “Our stories are eternal. We have a covenant from God with Abraham, and even though we've been through many hard times, we keep coming back, and God willing, it should continue.”
David, who works as an educator, is hopeful when it comes to Israel’s future. “We look at the Torah, the messages I’ve tried to bring across in the book, and we know that the end of the story will be good,” he says.
He adds, “We're living in one of the most incredible times in this country! We just have to open our eyes and look at what's happening around us. What we've achieved in this country is unbelievable. Today, for the first time, there are more Jews living in Israel than anywhere else in the world. We have an economy that defies economics.”
The secret of this success, explains David, “is that the Jewish people stay together, unified. King David taught us that unity is a national strategy. To him, it wasn't just a value. He understood that in order for us to survive and reach our destiny, we have to be united. And I think that's the greatest challenge that we face in Israel today, and no one is exempt from this, is how do we look beyond ourselves and make sure that, even though we might disagree with each other, that we still, at the end of the day, can sit around the table and live together. That's going to be the secret of our survival.”
David’s practical advice for achieving unity is to “just smile at people. Greet people warmly. When we meet other types of Jews, we have to open ourselves up a little bit to them, say hello to them. We just have to embrace them and show them a bit of warmth.”

questions.title: The "Sinn Féin Rabbi" Ireland's Footballers Forgot
questions.question: The "Sinn Féin Rabbi" Ireland's Footballers Forgot

answers.text:
Before Irish footballers bowed their heads through Israel's anthem, Ireland's chief rabbi hid Éamon de Valera from his enemies. That rabbi's grandson is Israel's president today.
Ireland’s dislike for Israel has reached the point where its national team’s soccer players literally can’t stand being on the field with Israelis.
In two recent Nations League matches against the Jewish state, Ireland’s players wore black armbands in protest over the war in Gaza, bowed their heads during Israel’s national anthem, and refused the customary pre-match handshakes.
The second match, played this past Sunday in Serbia and ending in a 1-1 draw after Ireland had won the first 3-0, came after the teams had been forced to play at neutral venues without spectators, an Irish player boycotted the first match, and a pre-contest press conference descended into a shouting match after an Israeli journalist accused Irish players of racist abuse, a charge Irish officials called “completely untrue,” before taking his microphone and abruptly ending the proceedings.
The historic irony of the Irish player’s ignorance runs deep. They seem unaware that there was a time when Ireland’s struggle for national independence inspired extraordinary sympathy from an unlikely quarter: its chief rabbi, whose grandson, named for him, serves as Israel’s president today.
Rabbi Isaac HaLevi Herzog, born in Łomża in Russian Poland, arrived in Ireland in 1915 in his late twenties. Herzog was a highly-educated polymath. In 1897, he studied oriental languages at the Sorbonne in Paris. He matriculated at the University of London in 1905, where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in classical and modern languages and mathematics in 1909. He then obtained a Masters of Arts in Semitics from the University of London in 1911, and a doctorate in literature from the same university in 1914.
Herzog first served as rabbi of Belfast (1915–19) and then moved to Dublin. Over roughly two decades in Ireland, Herzog became Chief Rabbi of the Irish Free State and a prominent advocate for its Jewish community, maintaining relationships with political and religious leaders, intervening on behalf of Jews seeking employment and religious accommodations, and defending Jewish religious practice. He also became unusually engaged with Irish public life, learning the Irish language and sympathizing with the movement for Irish independence.
This was hardly easy or safe work. Recalling this tumultuous time, Chaim Herzog, Rabbi Herzog’s son, who would become Israel’s president in 1983, recounted how one time, "I was approximately three years old at the time, and I remember a gunfight on the street in front of our house. From the window I could see a dead body being carted away. The activity aroused my curiosity and I went outside, fully exposed to the grave danger, in order to get a closer look. I felt a strong pull on my neck: my mother had run behind me and brought me back inside, strongly reprimanding me and commanding me to go to the bathroom in the basement, the most secure room in the house."
Rabbi Herzog’s support for Ireland’s independence led to a remarkable friendship with Éamon de Valera, one of the leading figures in the Irish struggle against British rule. He had commanded rebels in the Easter Rising of 1916, an armed revolt in Dublin that sought to establish an independent Irish republic; after its defeat, he emerged as one of the central figures of the independence movement. The struggle eventually produced the Irish Free State, while a bitter split over the terms of independence led to civil war.
Historian Dermot Keogh, in Jews in Twentieth-Century Ireland: Refugees, Anti-Semitism and the Holocaust (Cork University Press, 1998), reports that Rabbi Herzog sheltered Éamon de Valera while he was on the run during the Irish Civil War.
De Valera subsequently made the transition from revolutionary to constitutional politician, becoming head of the Irish government in 1932 and later president of Ireland. Herzog, meanwhile, became known as the “Sinn Féin Rabbi,” a reference to the principal Irish nationalist/republican political movement during the struggle for Irish independence.
Shaul Mayzlish, in his The Rabbinate in Stormy Days: The Life and Teachings of Rabbi Yitzhak Isaac HaLevi Herzog, recounts that Herzog’s scholarship not only impressed his freedom-fighting friend, it solved Jewish communal challenges as well. Mayzlish writes:
When opposition arose to kosher slaughter in Ireland, Rabbi Herzog’s calculated presentation to the governmental committee thwarted the initiative. The rabbi proved that kosher slaughter, which is so important for Jews, is humane and causes less anguish for the animals than other forms of slaughter… The members of the committee were so impressed that they decided that the city of Dublin would budget £4,200 for the building of a special slaughterhouse for the Jews. The chair of the committee wrote in the official account of the House of Representatives: "Blessed is the community that you represent, blessed is the community which has an advocate such as you, who presented the case from all its angles with such clarity.
When opposition arose to kosher slaughter in Ireland, Rabbi Herzog’s calculated presentation to the governmental committee thwarted the initiative. The rabbi proved that kosher slaughter, which is so important for Jews, is humane and causes less anguish for the animals than other forms of slaughter… The members of the committee were so impressed that they decided that the city of Dublin would budget £4,200 for the building of a special slaughterhouse for the Jews. The chair of the committee wrote in the official account of the House of Representatives: "Blessed is the community that you represent, blessed is the community which has an advocate such as you, who presented the case from all its angles with such clarity.
Meanwhile, Herzog and de Valera’s friendship endured through their respective career advancements. According to historian Dermot Keogh, de Valera consulted Herzog more than once while Ireland’s 1937 Constitution was being finalized; the Dictionary of Irish Biography likewise records that de Valera consulted Herzog about the constitution’s framing.
The former chief rabbi of Ireland was now chief rabbi of the Jewish state, welcoming the former Irish revolutionary who had become one of the founders and leading statesmen of modern Ireland.

The friendship then had a remarkable coda in the early years of the Jewish state. In July 1950, two years after Israel’s establishment, de Valera, who was then leader of the opposition in Ireland, visited Israel during a Holy Year pilgrimage. One of his first stops was a formal visit to Herzog, now Israel’s chief rabbi. Contemporary JTA reporting noted that de Valera “immediately paid a formal visit to Chief Rabbi Isaac Herzog, who was once the Chief Rabbi in Eire.” Herzog hosted a dinner in his honor that evening, attended by Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion and other Israeli leaders. The former chief rabbi of Ireland was now chief rabbi of the Jewish state, welcoming the former Irish revolutionary who had become one of the founders and leading statesmen of modern Ireland.
One can only hope that future footballers from the country that owes a debt of gratitude to its dedicated first Chief Rabbi will come to appreciate the contributions Jews made to their own country’s flourishing and freedom.

questions.title: NAZA's Biggest Claims, and Why the IDF Says They're Wrong
questions.question: NAZA's Biggest Claims, and Why the IDF Says They're Wrong

answers.text:
The controversial documentary accuses Israel's army of treating civilian lives as expendable. The IDF answers its claims one by one.
NAZA is the documentary everyone is talking about. At the Venice Film Festival on September 10, 2026, it earned a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation, and won the Special Jury Prize. Its charge is devastating: that Israel's army knowingly accepted massive civilian casualties in Gaza.
The film was commissioned by Britain's The Guardian and made by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who also collaborated on No Other Land, the Academy Award-winning documentary about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Abraham interviews 24 people who identify themselves as Israeli soldiers and intelligence officials. Each sits on a dark Tel Aviv rooftop at night, unnamed, with face and voice digitally altered. It makes for striking cinema.
The subject is collateral damage (nezek agavi in Hebrew, or "NAZA" for short): how much civilian harm Israel was willing to accept to strike military targets in Gaza. The interviewees claim the army allowed up to 500 civilian deaths for a single target (the figure the film's promotional material highlights), that artificial intelligence picked targets, and that Israeli strikes had a 15% error rate. The film includes no dissenting voices.
"NAZA" sounds a lot like "Nazi," and the film leans into it. At one point the camera lingers on a billboard of Claude Lanzmann, director of Shoah ("Holocaust" in Hebrew), the landmark Holocaust documentary. Even The Guardian's own review admits that one speaker invokes a comparison to Nazism "inevitably and glibly." Once NAZA finishes its theatrical run, The Guardian plans to stream it free on its website, permanently. There it will join Seven Jewish Children: A Play for Gaza, a harshly antizionist and antisemitic play that likens Jews to Nazis, which the paper also offers free, in perpetuity.
The film has quickly become a symbol of pro-Arab, anti-Israel feeling. Outside the Venice screening, antizionist activists flew kites, a deliberate echo of the incendiary kites Hamas has sent over the border from Gaza into Israel. And on October 1, 2026, at a screening in Delft, the Netherlands, October 7 survivor Sabine Taasa stood up to send a message to Abraham and Szor. Hamas terrorists murdered her husband, Gil, and their son, Or, on October 7, 2023. As Sabine began telling the Dutch audience how her family was killed, the crowd laughed and jeered: "Nobody cares!" "We don't want to hear it!" "Go away!" As she walked out, they roared "Shame on you!" at her back.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has released a detailed response in Hebrew and English. It says NAZA "presents a distorted, misleading, and disingenuous picture of the IDF's target planning and striking process," that its "narrative is based on substantial factual errors," and that the film "inverts reality." Here are the film's central claims, and the IDF's answers.
Collateral damage is a standard professional term, used by every law-abiding military in the world. Estimating expected harm to civilians is something international law requires. The IDF does it so commanders can decide whether a strike is lawful, add precautions, change the plan, or cancel it, "as IDF commanders did many times during the war." The film takes that careful effort and presents it as proof of indifference to civilian life.
This allegation is front and center in the film's trailer. The IDF's answer: it "has never planned, approved or carried out a strike in Gaza in which 500 civilians, or anything close to that number, were expected to be killed." No one has seriously claimed any IDF strike caused a toll anywhere near that, and the filmmakers offer no evidence for it.
"In the IDF, artificial intelligence does not determine whether an object or a person is designated as a target, nor whether a target is struck." Human analysts identify targets under set procedures, and an authorized intelligence officer approves them. Officers from several fields then review each proposed strike, and an operational commander makes the final decision under international law. Data tools simply help analysts sift intelligence they have already gathered.
As for the system called Lavender, the film treats it as a hit list. The IDF explains: "'Lavender' is not a list of targets approved to strike. As the IDF previously explained publicly, it is a database with the purpose of cross-referencing intelligence sources, in order to produce up-to-date layers of information on operatives in terror organizations in the Gaza Strip. A person's inclusion in 'Lavender' does not identify that person as a target, let alone authorize a strike against him."
This confuses who is allowed to approve a strike with permission to carry one out. Under IDF rules, higher estimates of civilian harm require sign-off from more senior officers, standard practice in Western militaries. A threshold like that "is not a permitted number of civilian casualties." Every commander must still judge each individual strike for proportionality. And no 200-casualty approval threshold for a military target "has ever applied or existed."
True, the IDF says, because international law requires exactly that: a civilian is a civilian at any age, and no life counts for less. In practice, "the presence of different categories of civilians, and children in particular, led commanders to cancel, postpone or replan strikes."
Several IDF units review strike outcomes, including reports of civilian harm, and the interviewees don't appear to have served in any of them. Those reviews led to debriefs on hundreds of incidents. Every suspected violation must be reported, and the Military Advocate General decides whether a criminal investigation is warranted.
IDF directives prohibit targeting civilians. Troops near the sites were permitted to fire only at military operatives and suspects posing an immediate threat. The sites operated in an active war zone, where armed militants deliberately blended into crowds. After several tragic incidents, the IDF held debriefs, issued new instructions, and added signs, physical barriers, and new access routes. Exceptional incidents went to the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism, and credible allegations of misconduct can lead to criminal investigations and indictments.
"An algorithm has never decided on a strike." A building must first be identified as a military target, and a warning never permitted commanders to ignore civilians still present. What the film calls "neighborhoods" were often Hamas combat compounds: clusters of buildings housing command posts, weapons, lookout and anti-tank positions, and tunnel shafts, all linked underground. Even then, each building had to be designated a military target on its own and assessed for proportionality.
The film goes further, painting Israeli soldiers as sadistic and malicious. The IDF responds: "The distinction between military operatives and civilians is fundamental to the IDF, its commanders and its binding directives during the fighting in Gaza. This distinction is unequivocally expressed in every protocol or directive that address targeting processes in the IDF." One interviewee's statement may reflect his personal feelings, the IDF says, but it in no way represents the army's approach.
Asked directly, one interviewee says yes. The IDF calls the accusation "outrageous and unfounded." Under international law, genocide requires the specific intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group. Polling anonymous non-experts who took no part in command decisions proves nothing. Israel's goals were to dismantle Hamas and create the conditions to bring the hostages home. The warnings, cancelled strikes, and humanitarian aid, the IDF notes, were measures to protect the very population Israel is accused of trying to destroy.
Beyond the specific claims, the IDF challenges the film's foundation: the assumption that its sources know what they're talking about. The anonymous interviewees appear to be speaking about matters "beyond their knowledge and competence." Abraham says he interviewed scores of soldiers, but with no names, or even ranks, there's no way to judge whether his damning portrait is accurate.
The speakers appear to be lower-level intelligence personnel. "Their accounts generally focus on limited, initial stages dealing with intelligence, rather than the much broader process of planning and approving strikes, which is the responsibility of operational bodies that manage and conduct targeting rather than the IDF's intelligence corps." An analyst might recall an early estimate of civilians near a target and assume it was final, without knowing the strike was later narrowed, the weapon or timing changed, or civilians evacuated after warnings. Many of the film's errors, the IDF says, "appear to stem from interviewees unfamiliar with the entire targeting process."
The film never shows the extensive network of military and civilian experts who weigh in on proposed strikes, including independent legal advisers, or those who kept humanitarian aid flowing into Gaza while fighting raged between Israel, Hamas, and its proxies.
Strangely, NAZA downplays Hamas's full-scale invasion of Israel on October 7, 2023, when about 6,000 fully armed and trained Hamas soldiers invaded Israel, with thousands of Gazan civilians following them. Without that context, the IDF says, the "filmmakers completely mischaracterize Israel's objectives in the war."
The film also skips over how "Hamas systematically and extensively embedded military operatives, weapons and military infrastructure within and beneath civilian areas, exploiting hospitals, UN facilities, schools and mosques for military purposes." Hamas used civilians as shields, and its fighters wore civilian clothes. That is the core of the issue the film claims to examine. As the IDF puts it, this context "explains why combat took place in urban areas and adversely affected civilians, as a result of Hamas' choice, not Israel's."
Also missing: what the IDF actually did to protect civilians. It cancelled or never approved many strikes because of the risk to civilians. It set up a dedicated Civilian Harm Mitigation Cell to issue warnings and track civilian movement across Gaza. And through COGAT (Coordination of Government Activities in the Territories), Israel facilitated the entry of more than 3.9 million metric tons of food into Gaza since October 2023.
Anonymous interviews may make for dramatic footage, but they undercut NAZA's claim to be a serious documentary in the tradition of Claude Lanzmann, whom the film deliberately invokes. Lanzmann's 1985 masterpiece Shoah is built on on-camera interviews with eyewitnesses who appear under their real identities, including perpetrators who had asked to stay anonymous.
"The filmmakers could have identified and avoided the substantial errors apparent in the film had they conducted adequate verification and corroboration in good faith," the IDF writes. "The end result shows they did not." The film cites no military directives, records, or other corroborating evidence. Its accounts of alleged strikes name no target, date, place, or casualty figures, so neither the IDF nor viewers can check them.
The filmmakers never approached the IDF for a response before release, a basic practice of investigative journalism, and declined its request for a copy of the film afterward. Some interviewees do "raise serious dilemmas posed by asymmetric warfare," the IDF acknowledges, but the film's "simplistic account does not treat them with the seriousness they deserve."
NAZA raises serious questions, but at heart it's a deeply unserious movie.
A hard-hitting documentary asks hard questions in the open. NAZA acts like it has something to hide, starting with the faces, voices, names, and jobs of the two dozen Israelis it features. It sidelines Hamas's strategy of embedding fighters in schools, hospitals, mosques, and apartment buildings to drive up civilian casualties. And, the IDF says, it "deepens this distortion of reality through manipulative editing of interviews and alluding to historical atrocities, while falsely and baselessly attributing malicious intentions to the IDF that the purported 'evidence' in the film does not substantiate."
The IDF doesn't dismiss the moral weight some interviewees describe. Decisions that may cost civilian lives are among the hardest any soldier faces, and the army expects its people to feel that weight. That burden, it says, reflects how seriously those decisions were made. It is no proof that they were unlawful.
Sadly, the IDF's response brings to mind the saying often attributed to Mark Twain: "A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes." NAZA portrays Israel as a monstrous nation bent on cruelty, and for Israel's detractors, no IDF report will change that.
As NAZA opens in more theaters, it's up to us to educate ourselves and others, and to answer its innuendo and half-truths with the facts: less cinematic, far more complicated, and true.

questions.title: Davidic Line Today
questions.question: Who are the descendants of King David today? I’m wondering what happened to the House of David. After the end of the Kingdom of Judah was there any memory what happened to King David’s descendants? Is there any family today which can trace its lineage to David – and whom the Messiah might descend from?

answers.text:
The End of the Davidic kingdom
There is no question that King David’s descendants are alive today. God promised David through Nathan the Prophet that the monarchy would never depart from his family (II Samuel 7:16). The prophets likewise foretell the ultimate coming of the Messiah, descendant of David, the “branch which will extend from the trunk of Jesse,” who will restore the Davidic dynasty and Israel’s sovereignty (Isaiah 11:1, see also Jeremiah 33:15, Ezekiel 37:25).
The Prophecy of the Davidic Dynasty
King David’s initial dynasty came to an end with the destruction of the First Temple and the Babylonian Exile. In an earlier expulsion King Jehoiachin was exiled by Nebuchadnezzar, together with his family and several thousand of the Torah scholars and higher classes (II Kings 24:14-16). Eleven years later the Temple was destroyed. The final king of Judah, Jehoiachin’s uncle Zedekiah, was too exiled to Babylonia. He was blinded and his children were executed (II Kings 25:7).
However, Jehoiachin and his descendants did survive in exile. Babylonian cuneiform records actually attest to Jehoiachin and his family receiving food rations from the government. I Chronicles 3:17-24 likewise lists several generations of his descendants (either 9 or 15 generations, depending on the precise interpretation of the verses), which would have extended well into the Second Temple era. (One was the notable Zerubbabel, grandson of Jehoiachin, who was one of the leaders of the return to Zion and the construction the Second Temple.)
In Babylonia, the leader of the Jewish community was known as the Reish Galuta (Aramaic for “head of the exile,” called the Exilarch in English). This was a hereditary position recognized by the Babylonian government. Its bearer was generally quite wealthy and powerful, well-connected to the government and wielding much authority over Babylonian Jewry.
King David's Lineage
According to Jewish tradition, the Exilarch was a direct descendant of Jehoiachin. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 5a) understands Genesis 49:10 – Jacob’s blessing to Judah that “the staff would not be removed from Judah” – as a reference to the Exilarchs in Babylonia, “who would chastise Israel with the staff,” i.e., who exercised temporal authority over the Jewish community. It stands to reason that these descendants of Judah were descendants of David’s house, who would have naturally been the leaders of the Babylonian community, in fulfillment of God’s promise to David that authority would always rest in his descendants.
There is also a chronological work, Seder Olam Zutta (an anonymous text from the early Middle Ages), which lists 39 generations of Exilarchs beginning with Jehoiachin. One of the commentators to Chronicles, the Vilna Gaon, states that the first one was Elionai of I Chronicles 3:23.
The position of Exilarch lasted for many centuries. The Reish Galuta is mentioned quite often in the Talmud. As can be expected, some were quite learned themselves, some deferred to the rabbis for religious matters, while some, especially in the later years, fought them and their authority tooth and nail.
Exilarchs existed well into the Middle Ages, throughout the period of the early medieval scholars known as the Gaonim. The last ones known to history was Hezekiah, who was killed in 1040 by the Babylonian authorities, although he was believed to have had sons who escaped to Iberia. There are likewise later historical references to descendants of the Exilarchs, especially in northern Spain (Catelonia) and southern France (Provence).
Beyond that, there is no concrete evidence as to the whereabouts of King David’s descendants. Supposedly, the great French medieval sage Rashi (R. Shlomo Yitzchaki) traced his lineage to King David, although on a maternal line. (In addition, Rashi himself only had daughters.) The same is said of Rabbi Yehuda Loewe of Prague (the Maharal). Since Ashkenazi Jews are so interrelated, this is a tradition, however dubious, shared by many Ashkenazi Jews today (my mother's family included). See also this past response about the kinship many of feel with King David and his story.
In any event, we do not need be concerned today how the Messiah son of David will be identified. He will be a prophet, second only to Moses. God Himself will select him and appoint him to his task. And he himself, with his Divine inspiration, will resolve all other matters of Jewish lineage (Maimonides Hilchot Melachim 12:3).
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Pedometer, Fitbit on Shabbat
questions.question: My family has become very health-conscious lately and we all have our own Fitbits which we wear all the time. It has really helped us maintain our health. Is there any issue with wearing it on Shabbat?

answers.text:
We may not wear such monitoring devices on Shabbat (unless a person has a life-threatening condition which requires constant surveillance). The reason is because the wearer is causing it to “work” on Shabbat by recording his motions. This is distinct from, say, the security cameras set up in many public places, since we are not interested in being filmed, but just in walking about regularly. Here, however, the wearer is interested in the readings. This is also different from a battery-operated watch and the like, which functions exactly the same throughout the day regardless of the person’s actions.
My wishes that in the merit of keeping Shabbat you and your family are blessed with good health for many years to come!
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Hamentaschen and Haman’s Three-Cornered Hat
questions.question: Is there a deeper meaning behind Haman’s 3-cornered hat? Why do we eat hamentaschen in memory of that of all things?

answers.text:
There is actually no classic source I am aware of which makes mention of Haman wearing a three-cornered hat. This is one of the suggestions given for the custom to eat the triangularly-shaped hamentaschen (or hamantashen) on Purim – that perhaps Haman wore such a hat and we eat them to commemorate his destruction. The earliest source I know of which mentions this theory is Otzar Dinnim u’Minhagim (Collection of Laws and Customs, by Rabbi J. D. Eisenstein, p. 336), originally published in New York in 1917. So it’s a perfectly good theory, but it’s really only a speculation. (It no doubt stems from the days when people imagined powerful goyim as wearing Napoleon-like three-cornered hats.)
The Yiddish word tasch means pouch or pocket. Thus, others suggest that the term is a reference to the Haman’s pockets – meaning the vast treasure he offered Ahasuerus for permission to wipe out the Jews (Esther 3:9). (Otzar Dinnim u’Minhagim suggests further that the many poppy seeds inside the “pocket” allude to the myriad coins he offered the king.)
In Modern Hebrew hamentaschen are known as “oznei haman” – “Haman ears” – and there exist several early references to such a name for them. As far as I know, this is equally speculative because there are no classic references to Haman having Vulcan ears (even though kiddie books often draw him as such), yet the same general idea emerges – of “destroying” Haman through our feasting. (It has been noted that in medieval times the ears of a condemned man would be cut off before his hanging. Thus, severed ears are reminiscent of Haman’s fate (I know, this makes them just a bit less appetizing). (Source: Sefer HaMoadim vol. 6 pp. 153-4.)
Another fairly plausible theory for the etymology of hamentaschen actually has grounds for it in Jewish custom. Hamentaschen were always classically filled with honeyed poppy seeds, mohn in Yiddish. And since tasch is a pocket, the treats might have originally been known as mohntaschen, which due to their association with Purim became known as hamentaschen (Sefer Matamim, Purim 2).
Why were these “poppy pockets” customarily eaten on Purim? It was in fulfillment of a custom to eat seeds on Purim. As the Book of Daniel (Ch. 1) records, when Daniel, Hanania, Mishael, and Azaria were forced into service in Nebuchadnezzar’s court, Daniel requested that they be given just seeds and water to eat so they wouldn’t have to defile themselves with non-kosher food. Their request was reluctantly granted, and they thrived on their limited (but fairly healthy) diet. The Talmud likewise records that Esther subsisted on seeds in order to keep kosher in the palace (Megillah 13a). In commemoration of this, the custom developed to eat seeds on Purim (Rema O.C. 695:2) – which later assumed this tasty form.
(Based on this, hamentaschen should really be filled with seeds – as they traditionally always were. The much more popular and exotic recipes of today – jams, chocolate, peanut butter, halva, caramel, etc. – were later innovations.)
Since Jewish customs are often so filled with meaning (as well as jelly), other fascinating allusions have been seen in hamentaschen. The treat is wrapped inside just as God’s providential Hand was hidden within events. Rather than performing open miracles, God quietly guided the course of events to bring about our salvation.
An equally fascinating suggestion is that Mordechai tried to rouse the Jews of Ahasuerus’s massive empire to repentance by sending out letters warning them of the dire events. But rather than sending the letters openly and drawing too much attention to his efforts, he sent them covertly, hidden inside of pastries! (Both explanations appear in the work Menucha u’Kedusha (2:20).)
An additional insight is offered based on the fact that Purim is a minor holiday. Unlike the major holidays, we are not restricted from performing labor on Purim. We thus eat a pastry with a treat hidden inside of it, signifying that though on the outside Purim is a regular day, it contains “treasures” – of sanctity and festivities – within. This is similar to the custom of eating kreplach (dumplings, dough filled with meat) on two other minor holidays – the eve of Yom Kippur and Hoshana Rabba (and some eat them on Purim as well). (Based on Ta’amei HaMinhagim 895.)
Finally, the three corners of the hamentaschen might allude to the three-way struggle between Ahasuerus, Haman and Esther or the three Patriarchs in whose merit we were saved (Otzar Dinnim u’Minhagim, based on Midrash, Sefer Matamim Purim 2).
For a more complete treatment of this interesting topic see here.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Musical Toys on Shabbat
questions.question: My two-year-old often gets ahold of his favorite musical toy on Shabbat and starts banging away at the keys. It certainly disturbs the serenity of Shabbat. Am I obligated to take it away from him? Am I even allowed to handle a noise-making toy myself on Shabbat? (If I can’t, it makes it much more difficult to take it away from my son.) What do you recommend?

answers.text:
There are actually several relevant issues here. But clearly, the ideal choice is to hide away such noisemakers before Shabbat so your child will not find them in the first place. This is what we attempt to do in the Rosenfeld household but often forget in the pre-Shabbat rush.
Now, if the situation does occur, there are a few relevant rules.
The first question is, does one have to stop his child from playing with such a toy? In your situation, the answer is no. Why not? Because of the following distinction. It is generally forbidden to cause another person to sin, even a baby (e.g. by feeding him non-kosher baby food) (Shulchan Aruch 343:1, Mishnah Berurah 4).
Here, however, your son took the toy on his own. Do you have to stop him? It depends on his age. There is an obligation on parents to instruct their children in observing the Torah’s commandments – and to stop them from transgressing a commandment. This obligation is known as chinuch, or “training.” However, it only begins when a child is old enough to appreciate that an act is truly the wrong thing to do, not just that he’ll obey your command not to do it. This is considered to begin at about 4 years of age (Mishnah Berurah 343:3, Children In Halacha, Ch. 1 II:B).
At 2, your son is below this age. It is certainly a nice idea to train him in correct behavior younger, and no doubt it will make your Shabbat more peaceful. Technically, however, you are not obligated to stop him. Thus, if you feel it’s not worth the scene trying to get his favorite toy away from him, you are not obligated.
The second issue you raised is known as muktzah – the restriction not to handle items which are not usable on Shabbat, such as money or a pencil, for fear you’ll unwittingly use them. This law extends to musical instruments as the Sages forbade playing music or using noisemakers on Shabbat (Shulchan Aruch & Rema 338:1).
If so, are you allowed to handle your child’s musical toy to take it away from him?
The answer to this is yes. The reason is because muktzah literally means “set aside” – something which is set aside on the Shabbat, not to be handled. Here, however, since your son is allowed to use his toy, it is not set aside (see Shulchan Aruch 308:52). Thus, you would be able to take it away from your child – or even better, take it away before he gets it.
One final important condition. Some musical toys cannot be lifted without inadvertently making music or noise. Such toys may not be moved on Shabbat since it is forbidden to use noisemakers on Shabbat.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Carrying Keys on Shabbat
questions.question: I’d like to know if there is any way I can carry my house key to the synagogue and back on Shabbat. The typical trick of hiding it under the mat just doesn’t feel so secure to me (we actually don’t have a mat anyway!). Is there any way to carry such a small item?

answers.text:
I assume first of all that your neighborhood does not have an eruv – a form of surrounding structure (usually composed of vertical posts and a surrounding wire) which permits carrying within it. Many Jewish communities worldwide have them.
It is forbidden to carry an item as small as a key on Shabbat. However, there is an old trick for doing so: making the key a part of your clothes.
The idea behind this is as follows. Although it is forbidden to carry in public on Shabbat, a person is obviously allowed to wear his clothes out of doors. Walking about wearing clothes is not “carrying” since the clothes are considered a part of the person. This extends to items which are clearly subordinate to one’s clothes – such as a belt, suspenders, safety pin, shoelaces. Even though you are not exactly “wearing” such things, they are helping your clothes stay on properly and so are considered a part of them (Rambam Hil’ Shabbat 18:17, Shulchan Aruch OC 301:39).
This would extend to a key as well if you “wear” it. How does one wear a key? There are two common methods. One is to fashion a tie clip out of a key, in which the top part of the clip is actually a key. Note that this would only work if your tie would be loose otherwise. If you are wearing a sweater or vest which holds down your tie, the clip would be serving no purpose and could not be considered a part of your clothes (The Shabbos Home, p. 130).
The second common method is to use your key as a belt buckle. This would involve removing the tongue of your belt and attaching your key in its place. Other similar methods might be replacing the buckle with a key, attaching a string to the other side, and threading the string through the hole at the top of the key to fasten your belt. As you can see, such methods require some ingenuity.
Note that such contraptions will typically have to be fashioned before Shabbat, since creating them may involve other forms of Shabbat labor – such as gluing or tying.
Note also that these methods will generally only work for a single key. I have seen people carry a ring with several keys attached to it in which one of the keys was holding their tie down. This is not correct. The entire addition to your clothes must be functioning as a part of them.
Make sure you are already “wearing” your key before leaving your house, and while entering it since it is forbidden to carry from a private to a public area. (You will then take the key off for a moment to lock/unlock your door, and then re-attach it before continuing.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Not Hungry for Third Meal (Seudah Shlishit)
questions.question: After the Shabbat day meal with that heavy cholent, I often have no appetite for the final meal. Is one required to eat it if he isn’t hungry?

answers.text:
Technically, no. Since the Shabbat meals are to enhance our enjoyment of Shabbat, one would not be required to eat if it pains him (Shulchan Aruch 291:1, Mishnah Berurah 3). Furthermore, there are opinions that the third meal does not require bread. If you’re not hungry enough for bread, grain foods are the next choice (cake, crackers, etc.). If that’s also too heavy, meat and fish are next, and as a last resort, you can eat fruit (OC 291:5).
However, according to all opinions bread is the first choice, and according to some, it is the only choice. (One should make the blessing on two whole loaves, as done at the first two meals (OC 291:4).) Thus, you should really make an effort not to overdo it at the main meal, making it impossible to eat bread at the final one. Regarding this, the codifiers of Jewish law apply the verse in Ecclesiastes (2:14) “A wise man looks ahead” (OC 291:1).
